title: Is Anthropic STEALING Your Data? (While You PAY FOR IT)
summary: Dan Eisler answers the question 'Is Anthropic stealing your data while you pay for it?' with a verdict grounded in public terms of service: no, they do not train on your data or own your outputs, but they do run anonymized aggregate analysis (their Cleo system) that maps which domains make money. He shows a chain of evidence that model labs compete with their customers once they see the trends (Cursor spawned Claude Code, Figma MCP usage spawned Claude Design, plus Claude Security and Claude Life Science). The solution is an 'AI sovereignty ladder': move from consumer subscriptions to commercial API, model clouds (AWS/GCP/Azure Foundry), owning your control plane with an LLM gateway, up to running open-weights models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, MiniMax, Qwen) on rented GPUs.
what_you_learn: You learn to reason about the privacy and competitive risks of routing agent traces through third-party model labs, and get a concrete tiered strategy (API vs model cloud vs self-hosted open weights) for protecting IP when building AI-agent systems. It teaches the key discrimination every agent engineer must make: commodity agent work vs IP-defensible agent work.

skills.name: Strategic Thinking
skills.description: Evaluate whether your agent traces, evals, and prompts are business-critical IP before sending them to a model lab.

skills.name: AI Vendor Management
skills.description: Accessing frontier models through AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex, or Azure Foundry so data is not sampled by the lab.

skills.name: Personal Automation
skills.description: Understanding Anthropic's privacy-preserving aggregated analysis system that turns prompts into market trends.

skills.name: Local Model Deployment
skills.description: Running models like Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, MiniMax, and Qwen on rented GPUs to own the model layer.

learnings.title: You pay for intelligence twice
learnings.detail: Dan opens with Satya Nadella's argument that you pay for AI once with money and again with the proprietary know-how you must reveal to make the model useful, plus Alex Karp of Palantir demanding control over compute, models, and 'alpha'. Microsoft even banned Fable 5 internally over its 30-day zero-data-retention (ZDR) retention policy.

learnings.title: The data tumbler makes your prompts a market map
learnings.detail: Prompts, agent traces, and workflows go into a 'data tumbler' where the lab anonymizes and aggregates them, like a coin tumbler. Legally it is no longer your data, but what comes out is still a map of the market: which domains (coding, design, legal) are valuable and growing.

learnings.title: The chain of evidence: labs enter verticals they observe
learnings.detail: Dan lists a pattern: heavy Cursor usage preceded Claude Code; Figma MCP usage preceded Claude Design; security usage preceded Claude Security; life science usage preceded Claude Life Science. 'One is a coincidence, four is a confirmation of the pattern.' He stresses this applies to all model labs, not just Anthropic.

learnings.title: Cleo powers the Anthropic Economic Index
learnings.detail: Anthropic's economic indexes, which break down AI usage by domain and socio-economic class, are built from Cleo, their 'aggregated privacy-preserving analysis' system. It is explicitly allowed in the terms of service, so every prompt can legally feed trend analysis.

learnings.title: Know the privacy controls you actually have
learnings.detail: In Claude.ai (Cmd+Shift+, then Settings, Privacy) you can uncheck 'Help improve our AI models' to opt out. Anthropic does not sell data to third parties and deletes on request, but Fable 5 has a mandatory 30-day retention window for cybersecurity review, which is why some enterprises banned it.

learnings.title: Not all customer classes get equal privacy
learnings.detail: Free-plan users are fully cooked: data is used for training. Pro and Max plans feed Cleo aggregation. Commercial tiers (Teams, Enterprise, API) have the strongest protections; Claude Code and other tools inherit the privacy level of the account type they run on.

learnings.title: Incentives, not goodwill, protect enterprise data
learnings.detail: The only thing keeping labs honest is that a single terms-of-service violation would trigger an enterprise exodus and kill the company. Incentives make every business decision, so understand the lab's incentive structure instead of trusting promises.

learnings.title: The verdict: four claims, only two survive
learnings.detail: Claim 1, labs see aggregate patterns: true. Claim 2, they train on your code and prompts: false per terms of service. Claim 3, they own your outputs: false, you own them. Claim 4, they compete with successful customer products: absolutely true. So: not stealing, but competing with customers using aggregate data.

learnings.title: Commodity agents vs IP agents and the trace test
learnings.detail: Commodity work (prototypes, CRUD, boilerplate, glue) can be sent to any lab without worry. IP agents hold your domain logic, evals, and user insights. The 80/20 test: 'If a competitor could read my full agent trace, would it matter?' The moment IP work enters an agent's context window, you are sending scarce compounding value to the lab.

learnings.title: The AI sovereignty ladder as the solution
learnings.detail: Tier 0 is a consumer subscription (lowest protection, aggregate sampling). Tier 1 is the commercial API. Tier 2 is a model cloud (AWS Bedrock, GCP Vertex, Azure AI Foundry) where Anthropic mounts its model and steps away, so your data is not sampled at all. Tier 3 is owning the control plane: a small VM plus a light LLM gateway that owns every trace and switches providers at will. Tier 4 is hybrid private: open-weights models on rented GPUs. Tier 5, owning GPU metal on-prem, is financially irrational for almost everyone.

learnings.title: Open weights are the escape hatch, not overseas APIs
learnings.detail: Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, MiniMax, and Qwen are commoditizing closed US labs and are the real exit strategy, but Dan is skeptical of deep-discount overseas API plans (including via OpenRouter) because their terms cannot be reliably enforced. Download the weights and mount them on GPUs you rent or own instead.

learnings.title: Best, mid, and worst cases share one defense
learnings.detail: Best case: labs stay platforms and keep serving models. Mid case (his bet): vertical competition continues. Worst case: anonymization becomes a legal alchemy that absorbs everything into lab IP. The defense is identical for all three: own the traces, own the evals, keep a second model passing on your IP-critical work, rent GPUs, and own the models.

key_points: Anthropic is not stealing your data, but they are competing with their customers using anonymized aggregate trends.
Cleo turns every prompt into market intelligence; usage data is the map of the money.
If a competitor could read your full agent trace, would it matter? That is the IP test.
If it is free, you are the product; commercial API and model clouds are meaningfully better protected.
Own the traces, own the evals, rent the GPUs, own the open-weights model.
Incentives protect your data, not goodwill; one ToS violation would be corporate suicide.
Climbing the sovereignty ladder is premature until you have real IP worth defending.
